learn.hook: A tabla player strikes the same drum gently and then hard, on the edge and then in the centre. The beats change in loudness and pitch. What is changing in the sound wave?
points: Sound is produced by vibrating objects and needs a medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel. It cannot travel through a vacuum.
In air, sound travels as a longitudinal wave: the particles vibrate back and forth along the direction of the wave, forming compressions (crowded regions) and rarefactions (spread-out regions).
Frequency (f) is the number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Time period T = 1 ÷ f. Higher frequency gives a higher pitch.
Amplitude is the maximum disturbance of the particles from their normal position. Larger amplitude gives a louder sound.

Wave speed = frequency × wavelength (v = f × λ). Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases. Humans hear about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz; lower is infrasound and higher is ultrasound.

example.q: Think it through: A tuning fork vibrates at 170 Hz. If sound travels at 340 m/s in air, what is the wavelength of the sound?
steps: Use v = f × λ, so λ = v ÷ f.

learn.reallife: A flute and a sitar playing the same note sound different because of their quality (timbre), and doctors use the high frequencies of ultrasound to see inside the body.

games.title: Can humans hear it?
items: A vibration of 5 Hz
A vibration of 15 Hz
A 256 Hz tuning fork
A 1000 Hz whistle
A 15 000 Hz beep
A 30 000 Hz dog whistle
A bat's call at 50 000 Hz
A medical scanner at 3 000 000 Hz

items.text: Regions where air particles are crowded together are called ___.
The SI unit of frequency is the ___.
A louder sound has a larger ___.
A higher frequency gives a higher ___.

quiz.q: Sound of frequency 170 Hz travels at 340 m/s in air. What is its wavelength in metres?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies speed and frequency instead of dividing

quiz.q: What is the SI unit of frequency?
quiz.explain: Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz); 1 Hz means one vibration per second.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the unit of frequency with the unit of loudness (decibel)

quiz.q: A girl's voice usually has a higher pitch than a man's. This means it has a
quiz.explain: Pitch depends on frequency. A shriller, higher-pitched voice has a higher frequency.
quiz.mistake: Thinks pitch depends on loudness (amplitude)

quiz.q: When you strike a dholak harder, the sound becomes louder. What has increased?
quiz.explain: A harder strike makes the drum skin vibrate with a larger amplitude, which we hear as a louder sound.
quiz.mistake: Thinks loudness depends on frequency

quiz.q: What is the normal range of hearing for humans?
quiz.explain: Humans hear roughly 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz (20 kHz). Sounds below are infrasound and sounds above are ultrasound.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the limits of human hearing

quiz.q: Two astronauts on the Moon cannot hear each other speak without radios, even standing close. Why?
options: There is no air on the Moon, and sound needs a medium
Sound is too fast on the Moon
quiz.explain: The Moon has almost no atmosphere. Sound needs a medium to travel, so it cannot pass through the vacuum between them.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sound can travel through empty space

quiz.q: A sound wave has a frequency of 50 Hz. What is its time period, in seconds?
quiz.mistake: Thinks the time period equals the frequency

quiz.q: In which medium does sound travel fastest?
quiz.explain: Particles in solids are tightly packed and strongly linked, so sound travels fastest in solids like steel. It cannot travel in a vacuum at all.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sound is fastest in air because we hear through air

teach.ask: Gappu chirps softly, then loudly, then in a squeaky voice: "What changes in my sound wave each time?"
teach.praise: Tweet! A louder chirp has a bigger amplitude, and a squeakier chirp has a higher frequency, which means a higher pitch!
teach.nudge: You told me what makes sound louder. What makes my voice squeaky and high-pitched?

learn.hook: Shout 'Hello!' towards a big hill and the hill shouts back a moment later. Ships use the same trick, with sounds we cannot hear, to measure how deep the ocean is!
points: Sound reflects from hard surfaces. An echo is the reflected sound heard separately from the original sound.
Our brain keeps a sound for about 0.1 s, so an echo is heard distinctly only if it returns after at least 0.1 s. With sound at 340 m/s, the reflecting surface must be at least 17 m away.
Reverberation is the persistence of sound in a hall because of repeated reflections. It is reduced by curtains, carpets, cushioned seats and sound-absorbing panels.
SONAR (Sound Navigation And Ranging) uses ultrasound. A ship sends ultrasound down, receives the echo from the sea bed and finds the depth d = (v × t) ÷ 2, since the sound goes down and comes back.
Bats and dolphins use echoes of ultrasound to find their way and catch prey. Doctors use ultrasound to make images of organs and of a baby in the womb.

example.q: Think it through: A ship's SONAR receives an echo from the sea bed 4 s after sending a pulse. If sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water, how deep is the sea?
steps: Total distance travelled by sound = v × t = 1500 × 4 = 6000 m.
This is the distance down AND back up.

learn.reallife: Indian Navy ships and research ships use SONAR to map the sea bed, and fishermen use fish-finders that work in the same way.

games.title: How SONAR measures depth
games.prompt: Arrange the steps from first to last
items: The transmitter on the ship sends ultrasound downwards
Ultrasound travels through the water
It reflects off the sea bed
The detector on the ship receives the echo
Depth is calculated as speed × time ÷ 2

games.title: Echoes: true or false?
items: An echo is reflected sound
Sound bounces off a surface and comes back to us as an echo.
You can hear a clear echo from a wall just 2 m away
The echo returns in far less than 0.1 s, so it merges with the original sound.
SONAR uses ultrasound
Ultrasound travels well in water and gives sharp, narrow beams.
Hanging heavy curtains in a hall increases reverberation
Soft materials absorb sound and reduce reverberation.
Bats use echoes of ultrasound to find insects in the dark
This is called echolocation.

quiz.q: A boy shouts near a cliff and hears the echo after 2 s. If sound travels at 340 m/s, how far away is the cliff?
quiz.explain: Sound travels 340 × 2 = 680 m in total, going to the cliff and back, so the cliff is 680 ÷ 2 = 340 m away.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by 2 for the return journey

quiz.q: Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, what is the minimum distance from a wall needed to hear a distinct echo?
quiz.explain: The echo must take at least 0.1 s for the round trip: 340 × 0.1 = 34 m in total, so the wall must be 34 ÷ 2 = 17 m away.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve the round-trip distance

quiz.q: What does SONAR stand for?
quiz.explain: SONAR stands for Sound Navigation And Ranging. It uses ultrasound echoes to find distances under water.
quiz.mistake: Confuses SONAR with RADAR, which uses radio waves

quiz.q: A ship's SONAR gets an echo from the sea bed after 4 s. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water. How deep is the sea?
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the sound travels down and back up

quiz.q: How can reverberation be reduced in a school auditorium?
options: By making the hall completely empty
By using curtains, carpets and sound-absorbing panels
quiz.explain: Soft, porous materials absorb sound instead of reflecting it, so repeated reflections die out quickly.
quiz.mistake: Thinks hard, bare surfaces reduce echoes

quiz.q: How do bats find their way and catch insects in the dark?
options: They see well in total darkness
They smell the insects from far away
They send out ultrasound and listen for the echoes
They use infrasound from the ground
quiz.explain: Bats send out high-pitched ultrasound squeaks, and the echoes tell them where obstacles and insects are. This is echolocation.
quiz.mistake: Thinks bats depend on their eyesight at night

quiz.q: What is a common medical use of ultrasound?
quiz.explain: Ultrasound scanners send ultrasound into the body and use the echoes to make images of organs, or of a baby in the womb.
quiz.mistake: Confuses ultrasound scans with X-rays

quiz.q: Why are the ceilings of many concert halls curved?
options: To reflect sound evenly to all parts of the hall
quiz.explain: Curved ceilings and soundboards reflect sound so that it spreads evenly to the audience.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the shape of a hall with reflection of sound

teach.ask: Gappu shouts at a big rock: "Hello?" The rock says "hello" back! "Is the rock talking to me?"
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! The rock isn't talking. My sound bounced off it and came back as an echo, which I can hear separately if the rock is far enough away!
teach.nudge: My chirp travelled to the rock. What happened to it when it hit the hard rock?

learn.hook: Your ear can pick up a whisper and a thunderclap, and it contains the smallest bone in your whole body, smaller than a grain of rice!
points: Outer ear: the pinna collects sound and sends it through the ear canal (auditory canal) to the eardrum.

Middle ear: the eardrum (tympanic membrane) vibrates with the sound. Three tiny bones, the hammer (malleus), anvil (incus) and stirrup (stapes), pass on and amplify these vibrations. The stirrup is the smallest bone in the human body.
The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the throat and keeps the air pressure equal on both sides of the eardrum.
Inner ear: the snail-shaped cochlea turns the vibrations into electrical signals, which the auditory nerve carries to the brain. The brain interprets them as sound.
Care for your ears: keep earphone volume low, take breaks, avoid very loud noise and never poke anything sharp into the ear.

example.q: Think it through: While driving up a hill road to Shimla, Tanya's ears feel blocked and then 'pop' when she swallows. Why?
steps: As the car climbs, the outside air pressure drops.
For a while, the air pressure in the middle ear is higher than outside, so the eardrum is pushed outwards and feels blocked.
Swallowing opens the Eustachian tube, which joins the middle ear to the throat.
Air moves through it, the pressures become equal and the ear 'pops'.
example.answer: The Eustachian tube opened and equalised the air pressure on both sides of the eardrum.

learn.reallife: Audiologists test hearing with sounds of different frequencies, and hearing aids amplify sounds for people with hearing loss.

games.title: The path of sound through the ear
games.prompt: Arrange from outside to the brain
items: Pinna collects the sound
Sound travels down the ear canal
Eardrum vibrates
Hammer, anvil and stirrup amplify the vibrations
Cochlea changes vibrations into electrical signals
Auditory nerve carries signals to the brain

games.title: Match the ear part to its job

quiz.q: Which part of the ear collects sound from the surroundings?
quiz.explain: The pinna is the outer, visible part of the ear. Its shape helps gather sound into the ear canal.
quiz.mistake: Thinks hearing begins inside the ear at the cochlea

quiz.q: The eardrum is also called the
quiz.explain: The eardrum is a thin, stretched membrane called the tympanic membrane. It vibrates when sound waves reach it.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the names of different ear parts

quiz.q: Which three tiny bones are in the middle ear?
quiz.explain: The hammer (malleus), anvil (incus) and stirrup (stapes) pass on and amplify the vibrations of the eardrum.
quiz.mistake: Lists ear parts that are not bones

quiz.q: What is the smallest bone in the human body?
quiz.explain: The stirrup in the middle ear is the smallest bone in the human body.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the smallest bone is in the fingers or toes

quiz.q: Which part of the ear changes vibrations into electrical signals?
quiz.explain: The fluid-filled cochlea in the inner ear has sensitive cells that change vibrations into electrical signals.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the eardrum sends signals directly to the brain

quiz.q: Which nerve carries sound signals from the ear to the brain?
quiz.explain: The auditory nerve carries signals from the cochlea to the brain. The optic nerve is for the eye, the olfactory nerve for smell.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the nerves of the different sense organs

quiz.q: What is the job of the Eustachian tube?
options: To keep the air pressure equal on both sides of the eardrum
To carry signals to the brain
quiz.explain: It links the middle ear to the throat, so air can move in or out to balance the pressure, for example on a hill road or in a plane.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that the middle ear is connected to the throat

quiz.q: Which is the best habit for protecting your hearing?
options: Listening to music at full volume
Keeping earphone volume low and taking breaks
Standing next to loudspeakers at events
quiz.explain: Loud sound over a long time can damage the sensitive cells of the cochlea. Low volume and breaks protect them.
quiz.mistake: Does not realise that loud sounds can damage hearing permanently

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head at a song: "How does the music get from the radio into my brain?"
teach.praise: Tweet! Sound enters the ear canal, the eardrum vibrates, the tiny bones and cochlea turn it into signals, and the auditory nerve takes them to my brain!
teach.nudge: After the eardrum vibrates, how does the message finally reach my brain?
